figures.shows: Four-layer TFIM VQE best energy error per seed (0, 1, 2) for Adam and for the best QNM variant, with the variant selected; Adam errors 4.832e-7, 5.142e-7, 1.218e-6 (mean 7.385e-7); best QNM errors 1.529e-7, 1.509e-7, 1.334e-7 (mean 1.457e-7); QNM-layer selected on all three seeds.
figures.confirmed_by: As Table 1 shows, QNM improves the best energy error on all three seeds and reduces the mean error by 80.3%.

figures.shows: Weighted generalized QAOA-MaxCut, n = 10 nodes, 23 edges, depth 3: achieved expected cut Vm, ratio Vm/C* and optimality gap for Adam, Muon, DA-Muon, QNG, QNM-layer, QNM-global, QNM-gate and DA-QNM-gate (gap 0.4625, 0.7243, 0.7205, 0.2634, 0.2832, 0.2707, 0.01451, 0.01368).
figures.confirmed_by: QNG reduces Adam’s optimality gap by 43.0%, showing the benefit of quantum geometry.

figures.shows: Horizontal bars, optimizer (y: DA-QNM-gate, QNM-gate, QNG, QNM-global, QNM-layer, DA-Muon, Muon) against gap reduction relative to Adam in percent (x, about -60 to 100). Bar labels: 97.0, 96.9, 43.0, 41.5, 38.8 (all positive) and -55.8, -56.6 for DA-Muon and Muon (negative, i.e. a larger gap than Adam).
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 1 summarizes the ablation: Muon/DA-Muon worsen the Adam gap, QNG improves it, and the largest gains occur only when QFIM preconditioning is followed by gate-structured spectral normalization.

figures.shows: Grouped bars, value (y, 0 to about 10.5) for two metrics (x: Cond. number, Effective rank), before (blue) and after (orange hatched) polar mixing. Condition number about 10 before and about 1.9 after, labeled -81.7%; effective rank about 2.2 before and about 2.8 after, labeled +27.9%. The caption gives 10.13 to 1.85 and 2.22 to 2.84.
figures.confirmed_by: Figure 2 shows an 81.7% reduction in active condition number and a 27.9% increase in effective rank, consistent with the spectral-floor mechanism in Section 4.

figures.shows: Iris classification after 120 steps, mean test accuracy with standard error over three train-test splits, for Adam, Muon, Diag-QNM, DA-QNM. Setosa vs. rest: 0.9111, 0.9407, 0.9481, 0.9407. Versicolor vs. virginica: 0.8222, 0.8333, 0.8556, 0.8762. Best per task in bold: Diag-QNM on setosa, DA-QNM on versicolor.
figures.confirmed_by: Table 3 shows that quantum-geometric QNM variants improve mean accuracy over Adam on both tasks.

figures.shows: VQE architecture: TFIM Hamiltonian box (sum of Z Z coupling and X field terms on n qubits, 4 qubits drawn), a parameterized ansatz of L layers each with RY and RZ rotations and CNOT entanglers on 4 qubits, measurement and energy estimation, a classical optimizer loop updating theta, and a layer-wise parameter organization as a tensor of layers by qubits by parameters per qubit (r = 2 for RY and RZ). No numerical results.
figures.confirmed_by: Fig. 3 summarizes the VQE experimental workflow used in our simulations, including state preparation, Hamiltonian expectation evaluation, optimizer update, and the DA-QNM-specific QFIM and spectral normalization steps.

figures.shows: Weighted QAOA architecture: a weighted MaxCut instance graph on 5 nodes with example edge weights (0.8, 1.2, 0.5, 1.0, 0.7, 1.5) drawn as an illustration, a generalized QAOA circuit of p layers alternating cost unitary UC(Gamma) and mixer unitary UM(B), measurement and cut-value estimation, a classical optimizer updating Gamma and B, and the gate-wise parameter matrices Gamma (p by |E|, cost angles) and B (p by |V|, mixer angles). The drawn 5-node graph is not the 10-node experimental instance.
figures.confirmed_by: Fig. 4 summarizes the generalized QAOA workflow used in the weighted MaxCut experiment and highlights the parameter blocks on which gate-structured QNM operates.

figures.shows: Normalized singular value (y, 0 to about 1.1) for four active singular directions (x: 1 to 4), before (blue) and after (orange hatched) polar mixing, for a representative QNM-gate momentum block. Before: about 1.0, 0.31, 0.18, 0.10. After: about 1.0, 0.82, 0.65, 0.54.
figures.confirmed_by: Fig. 5 complements the main spectral summary by displaying the singular values themselves.

papers.what_it_is: A theory and simulation paper that proposes Quantum Natural Muon (QNM) and its distance-aware form DA-QNM, optimizers that apply blockwise polar normalization after damped quantum Fisher preconditioning, with descent and stationarity proofs and small simulations on VQE, weighted QAOA-MaxCut and Iris classification.

assertions.value: The authors define Quantum Natural Muon (QNM) as a spectral natural-gradient framework that applies polar normalization to circuit-semantic parameter blocks after damped quantum Fisher preconditioning, mixing each block with a Frobenius-matched polar factor.
quotes: We introduce Quantum Natural Muon (QNM), a spectral naturalgradient framework that applies polar normalization to circuit-semantic parameter blocks after damped quantum Fisher preconditioning.
It then reshapes the momentum according to circuit semantics and mixes each block with a Frobenius-matched polar factor, balancing its active spectrum without replacing its blockscale information.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its method in the abstract and Section 1.

assertions.value: The authors define DA-QNM as the distance-aware realization of QNM: it normalizes the spectral-natural direction and controls the final displacement with an adaptive radius, and they state that the radius rule itself is not claimed as new.
quotes: Its distance-aware realization, DA-QNM, normalizes the resulting spectral-natural direction and controls the final displacement with an adaptive radius; the radius rule itself is not claimed as new.
We do not claim that the radius rule itself is new; rather, DA-QNM uses distance-aware scaling to control the step length after QFIM-preconditioned spectral
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition and its own statement of what is not claimed as new.
assertions.reader_inference: The radius rule is credited to Distance-Aware Muon (Demidovich et al., 2026) in the introduction.

assertions.value: The authors define DA-QNM to accumulate momentum in natural-gradient space, as an exponential moving average of the damped natural-gradient vector with a coefficient beta, so that spectral normalization acts on a quantum-geometrically calibrated direction rather than on the raw Euclidean gradient.
quotes: DA-QNM accumulates momentum in natural-gradient space:
Thus, the subsequent spectral normalization acts on a quantum-geometrically calibrated direction rather than on the raw Euclidean gradient.

assertions.value: The paper proves (Theorem 6, auxiliary) that for the fixed-scale update with step gamma, if the directions satisfy an alignment bound with constant nu and a norm bound with constant B and gamma is small enough, the minimum squared gradient norm is O(1/T ); the paper states this is auxiliary and not the main guarantee for the implemented algorithm.

quotes: Theorem 6 (Fixed-scale nonconvex stationarity). Assume C is L-smooth and lower bounded by C⋆. Consider updates of the form θt+1 = θt − γdt. Suppose the update directions satisfy
⟨gt, dt⟩ ≥ ν∥gt∥22, ∥dt∥2 ≤ B∥gt∥2
so the minimum stationarity measure is also O(1/T ).
Theorem 6 is auxiliary. The main stationarity guarantee for the implemented algorithm is Theorem 4, which applies to the normalized distance-aware update generated by Algorithm 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: The step-size condition and the displayed bound are broken across lines in the text layer, so the full statement could not be quoted verbatim.

assertions.value: The authors state that the conditions in Corollaries 2 and 3 are sufficient, not necessary, and that in practice a substantially larger alpha may work because the polar perturbation is often aligned with the natural-gradient block.
quotes: The conditions in Corollaries 2 and 3 are sufficient, not necessary.
In practice, substantially larger α may work because the polar perturbation is often aligned with the natural-gradient block.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim about practice, given without evidence.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiments use alpha 0.3, which satisfies the sufficient condition 2α below mu over Lambda only if mu over Lambda exceeds 0.6; the paper reports no value of mu over Lambda, so whether the guarantees cover the reported runs is not stated.

assertions.value: The authors state that the VQE experiment uses a periodic transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian with a four-layer hardware-efficient ansatz, that the reported metric is the best energy error over the optimization trajectory, and that the exact ground-state energy comes from classical diagonalization.
quotes: We consider VQE for a periodic transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian using a four-layer hardware-efficient ansatz.
The exact ground-state energy E⋆ is computed by classical diagonalization, and the reported metric is the best energy error achieved over the optimization trajectory,
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no qubit count, coupling or field values, step count or learning rate for VQE. Figure 3 draws four qubits as an illustration; the text does not say the experiment used four.

assertions.value: The authors state that the main text reports the best QNM variant per seed, chosen among layer-, gate- and global-block variants, and that QNM-layer is selected for all three tested seeds.
assertions.anchor: Table 1 caption, Section 5.1, p.7; Appendix C.1, p.22
quotes: Table 1: Four-layer TFIM VQE. “Best QNM” selects among layer-, gate-, and global-block variants; QNMlayer is selected for all seeds.
The main text reports the best QNM variant per seed; in the current runs, QNM-layer is selected for all three tested seeds.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The QNM column is a minimum over three variants per seed, while Adam is one configuration, so the comparison favors QNM by selection. The paper reports the per-variant errors for gate and global blocks nowhere.

assertions.value: The authors report, on a four-layer TFIM VQE over three seeds, a mean best energy error of 7.385 × 10−7 for Adam and 1.457 × 10−7 for the best QNM variant, and that QNM reduces the mean error by 80.3%.
quotes: As Table 1 shows, QNM improves the best energy error on all three seeds and reduces the mean error by 80.3%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with three seeds.
assertions.reader_inference: Three seeds, no standard errors; both errors are already near 1e-7, so the absolute difference is tiny. Reader check: (7.385 - 1.457) / 7.385 = 80.3%.

assertions.value: The authors report per-seed best energy errors on the four-layer TFIM VQE: for seeds 0, 1 and 2 Adam reaches 4.832 × 10−7, 5.142 × 10−7 and 1.218 × 10−6, and the best QNM variant reaches 1.529 × 10−7, 1.509 × 10−7 and 1.334 × 10−7.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors state that the generalized QAOA experiment uses a weighted MaxCut instance with n = 10 nodes, 23 edges and depth p = 3, with exact optimum C⋆ = 17.818521 computed by exhaustive enumeration.
quotes: We evaluate generalized QAOA on weighted MaxCut with n = 10 nodes, |E| = 23 edges, depth p = 3, and exact optimum C⋆ = 17.818521, computed by exhaustive enumeration.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not give the edge weights of the instance or say how they were drawn.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QAOA cost and mixer parameters form a cost-angle matrix of 3 by 23 indexed by depth and edge and a mixer-angle matrix of 3 by 10 indexed by depth and node, and that heterogeneous edge weights can induce anisotropy across the edge-indexed update.
quotes: The cost and mixer parameters form Γ ∈ R3×23 and B ∈ R3×10, indexed by depth–edge and depth–node, respectively.
Heterogeneous edge weights directly affect the cost generators and can induce anisotropy across the edge-indexed Γ update, making this a natural test of semantic block choice.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup (the anisotropy remark is the authors' motivation).

assertions.value: The authors state that the weighted QAOA experiment is a controlled component diagnostic on one instance and not a broad QAOA benchmark, that all methods use the same weighted instance and initialization seed, and that they do not claim broad QAOA dominance from one instance.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2, p.7; Appendix C.2, p.22 to p.23
quotes: We use this instance as a controlled component diagnostic rather than a broad QAOA benchmark.
same weighted instance and the same initialization seed. The purpose of this experiment is not to claim broad QAOA dominance from one instance,
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper itself states the scope limit of its QAOA measurement in Section 5.2 and Appendix C.2.
assertions.reader_inference: Appendix C.6 gives seed 0 for the representative run, so every QAOA number in the paper comes from one instance and one seed.

assertions.value: The authors report that the DA-QNM QAOA run used CPU double-precision simulation, seed 0, 180 optimization steps, learning rate 0.04, Adam learning rate 0.05, momentum coefficient β = 0.9, QFIM damping λ = 0.05, QFIM refresh period 3, maximum update norm 0.05 and polar-mixing coefficient α = 0.3.
quotes: The DA-QNM QAOA implementation used CPU-based double-precision simulation, seed 0, 180 optimization steps, learning rate 0.04, Adam learning rate 0.05, momentum coefficient β = 0.9, QFIM damping λ = 0.05, QFIM refresh period 3, maximum update norm 0.05, and polar-mixing coefficient α = 0.3.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: Hyperparameters of Muon, DA-Muon and QNG and any tuning procedure are not given. A QFIM refresh period of 3 means the QFIM is not recomputed each step.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the weighted QAOA instance, QNG reduces the Adam optimality gap by 43.0%, with a final gap of 0.2634 against 0.4625 for Adam.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2 and Table 2, p.7; Section 1, p.2
quotes: QNG reduces Adam’s optimality gap by 43.0%, showing the benefit of quantum geometry.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one instance and one seed.
assertions.reader_inference: Single seed, single instance, no error bars. The row labels are on separate lines in the text layer; the page image confirms the rows are Adam and QNG.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the weighted QAOA instance, gate-structured QNM reduces the Adam optimality gap by 96.9%, with expected cut 17.804015, approximation ratio 0.999186 and gap 0.01451.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2 and Table 2, p.7; Section 1, p.2
quotes: QNM-gate increases this reduction to 96.9%, whereas QNM-layer/global remain near QNG,
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one instance and one seed.
assertions.reader_inference: Single seed, single instance. The gate-wise block structure matches the edge and node parameter matrices that the paper itself chose, so the match between block choice and structure is by construction.

assertions.value: The authors report that DA-QNM-gate further reduces the QNM-gate gap by 5.7%, reaching expected cut 17.804840, ratio 0.999232 and gap 0.01368, which is a 97.0% reduction of the Adam gap.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.2 and Table 2, p.7; Section 1, p.2
quotes: DA-QNM-gate further reduces the QNM-gate gap by 5.7%,
while gate-structured QNM reduces it by 96.9% and DA-QNM by 97.0%.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one instance and one seed.
assertions.reader_inference: The gap difference between QNM-gate and DA-QNM-gate is 0.00083 on a single run, so no uncertainty is available to judge it.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the weighted QAOA instance QNM-layer and QNM-global stay near QNG, with gaps 0.2832 and 0.2707 against 0.2634 for QNG, and state that this shows spectral normalization depends critically on circuit-semantic block choice.
quotes: whereas QNM-layer/global remain near QNG, showing that spectral normalization depends critically on circuit-semantic block choice.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one instance and one seed.
assertions.reader_inference: The layer and global variants have gaps slightly above QNG, so they are marginally worse than QNG alone in this run.

assertions.value: The authors report that on the weighted QAOA instance Muon and DA-Muon have worse optimality gaps than Adam, 0.7243 and 0.7205 against 0.4625, and state that neither Euclidean spectral normalization nor distance-aware scaling alone explains the gain.
quotes: while DAMuon performs worse than Adam; neither Euclidean spectral normalization nor distance-aware scaling alone explains the gain.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one instance and one seed; a negative measured result is not a stated limit.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not say whether Muon was tuned. A Muon worse than Adam on one instance is a weak baseline result.

assertions.value: The authors state that the dominant improvement comes from gate-aligned spectral normalization after QFIM preconditioning, with radius control providing a smaller additional benefit.
quotes: The dominant improvement therefore comes from gate-aligned spectral normalization after QFIM preconditioning, with radius control providing a smaller additional benefit.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's interpretation of one instance and one seed.

assertions.value: The authors state that Euclidean, layer-wise and global spectral variants do not obtain the same gain as gate-structured QNM, showing that spectral normalization alone is insufficient.
quotes: In contrast, Euclidean, layer-wise, and global spectral variants do not obtain the same gain, showing that spectral normalization alone is insufficient.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's interpretation of one instance and one seed.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 1: the bar labels give the optimality-gap reduction relative to Adam as about 97.0% for DA-QNM-gate, about 96.9% for QNM-gate, about 43.0% for QNG, about 41.5% for QNM-global, about 38.8% for QNM-layer, about -55.8% for DA-Muon and about -56.6% for Muon.
quotes: Figure 1: Optimality-gap reduction relative to Adam on weighted QAOA-MaxCut. QNM-gate and DA-QNMgate achieve 96.9% and 97.0% reductions, respectively.
Figure 1 summarizes the ablation: Muon/DA-Muon worsen the Adam gap, QNG improves it, and the largest gains occur only when QFIM preconditioning is followed by gate-structured spectral normalization.
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read from a figure is never suggested high; one instance, one seed.
assertions.reader_inference: The QNM-layer and QNM-global reductions appear only in the figure labels. Reader check: from Table 2 gaps, (0.4625 - 0.2832) / 0.4625 = 38.8% and (0.4625 - 0.2707) / 0.4625 = 41.5%, matching the labels. The Muon and DA-Muon reductions are negative, matching the worse gaps in Table 2.

assertions.value: The authors define the diagnostics as the active condition number, the ratio of the largest to the smallest active singular value, and the effective rank, the exponential of the entropy of the normalized singular values, both tracked on structured momentum blocks.
quotes: we track the active condition number κact(M) = σ1(M)/σr(M) and effective rank reff (M) = exp(− i pi log pi), where pi = σi/ j σj, of structured momentum blocks.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of its diagnostics.

assertions.value: The authors report that polar mixing reduces the measured active condition number of a representative structured update from 10.13 to 1.85, an 81.7% reduction.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.3 and Figure 2, p.8; Section 1, p.2
quotes: Figure 2: Polar mixing reduces the active condition number from 10.13 to 1.85 and increases effective rank from 2.22 to 2.84.
Figure 2 shows an 81.7% reduction in active condition number and a 27.9% increase in effective rank, consistent with the spectral-floor mechanism in Section 4.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one representative block.
assertions.reader_inference: One representative block of the QAOA run; the paper does not say at which iteration or in which block it was taken. Reader check: (10.13 - 1.85) / 10.13 = 81.7%.

assertions.value: The authors report that polar mixing increases the effective rank of a representative structured update from 2.22 to 2.84, a 27.9% increase.
assertions.anchor: Section 5.3 and Figure 2, p.8; Section 1, p.2
quotes: Figure 2: Polar mixing reduces the active condition number from 10.13 to 1.85 and increases effective rank from 2.22 to 2.84.
Figure 2 shows an 81.7% reduction in active condition number and a 27.9% increase in effective rank, consistent with the spectral-floor mechanism in Section 4.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one representative block.
assertions.reader_inference: Reader check: 2.84 / 2.22 = 1.279, matching 27.9%.

assertions.value: Read from Figure 5: for a representative QNM-gate momentum block with four active singular directions, the normalized singular values are about 1.0, about 0.31, about 0.18 and about 0.10 before polar mixing and about 1.0, about 0.82, about 0.65 and about 0.54 after, so the spectrum becomes flatter and the dominant direction is unchanged.
assertions.anchor: Figure 5, Appendix C.3, p.25; Appendix C.3, p.23
quotes: Before mixing, the spectrum is anisotropic, with a few dominant directions and several weak active singular directions. After mixing, the spectrum becomes flatter: weak active directions are lifted while the dominant structured directions are preserved.
This provides empirical evidence that QNM mitigates spectral collapse in circuit-semantic update blocks, consistent with the predicted mechanism.
assertions.certainty_reason: A value read from a figure is never suggested high.
assertions.reader_inference: Reader checks from bar heights read by eye: the condition number is about 1/0.10 = 10 before and about 1/0.54 = 1.9 after, consistent with Figure 2 (10.13 to 1.85). The effective rank computed from these four values is about 2.8 before and about 3.9 after, not the 2.22 and 2.84 of Figure 2; the paper does not say the two figures show the same block, so the figures may show different blocks.

assertions.value: The authors state that the supervised experiments use a two-qubit data-reuploading classifier with a 2 × 2 × 3 parameter tensor organized by layer, qubit and rotation axis, so the flattened parameter vector has dimension 12, with an empirical supervised QGT/QFIM.
quotes: We use a twoqubit data-reuploading classifier with a 2 × 2 × 3 parameter tensor organized by layer, qubit, and rotation axis, together with an empirical supervised QGT/QFIM.
Equivalently, the flattened parameter vector θ has dimension d = 2 · 2 · 3 = 12.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Iris tasks are setosa versus the other two classes and versicolor versus virginica, with stratified train-test splits, PCA fit only on the training split to two dimensions, and the two principal coordinates rescaled to rotation angles by a scaling map fit on the training split.
quotes: The first task separates setosa from the other two classes, while the second task separates versicolor from virginica after removing setosa examples.
To avoid data leakage, PCA is fit only on the training split.
The scaling map is fit on the training split and then reused on the test split, again to prevent test information from entering the training pipeline.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors define the empirical supervised QFIM as the mini-batch average of the real part of the input-conditioned quantum geometric tensor, state that the readout parameters are treated as Euclidean and excluded from the circuit QGT block, and define Diag-QNM as the diagonal approximation of this matrix followed by damped preconditioning and Muon-style spectral normalization.
quotes: The empirical supervised QFIM used by QNM is the mini-batch average of the real part of this input-conditioned QGT:
The readout parameters a and b, when optimized, are treated as ordinary Euclidean readout parameters and are not included in the circuit QGT
Diag-QNM uses a diagonal approximation of Ftsup, followed by damped preconditioning and Muon-style spectral normalization on the trainable parameter tensor.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definitions for its supervised experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: Three definitions in one entry; the coordinator may split them.

assertions.value: The authors report, after 120 steps and over three train-test splits, mean test accuracy on setosa versus rest of 0.9111 ± 0.0128 for Adam, 0.9407 ± 0.0148 for Muon, 0.9481 ± 0.0196 for Diag-QNM and 0.9407 ± 0.0148 for DA-QNM.
quotes: Table 3: Iris classification after 120 steps: mean test accuracy ± standard error over three train–test splits.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with three splits.
assertions.reader_inference: Muon and DA-QNM have identical mean and standard error (0.9407 ± 0.0148), and all four methods are within about two standard errors of each other, so the ranking is not resolved by three splits. Muon, which has no quantum geometry, also beats Adam here.

assertions.value: The authors report, after 120 steps and over three train-test splits, mean test accuracy on versicolor versus virginica of 0.8222 ± 0.0222 for Adam, 0.8333 ± 0.0385 for Muon, 0.8556 ± 0.0401 for Diag-QNM and 0.8762 ± 0.0222 for DA-QNM.
quotes: Table 3: Iris classification after 120 steps: mean test accuracy ± standard error over three train–test splits.
DA-QNM performs best on the harder versicolor-versus-virginica task (0.8762 versus 0.8222)
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with three splits.
assertions.reader_inference: The DA-QNM minus Adam difference of 0.054 is about two standard errors of Adam (0.0222) on three splits.

assertions.value: The authors state that they do not interpret the small Iris study as a broad supervised-QML benchmark, and that the experiment is intentionally small-scale and not meant to claim state-of-the-art supervised quantum classification performance on Iris.
quotes: We do not interpret this small Iris study as a broad supervisedQML benchmark.
This experiment is intentionally small-scale. Its purpose is not to claim state-of-the-art supervised quantum classification performance on Iris,
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper itself states the scope limit of its Iris measurement in Section 5.4 and Appendix C.4.

assertions.value: The authors state that the finite-shot experiments train each method for 70 optimization steps over five independent seeds, with training on exact expectation values or on finite-shot sampled observables and final test metrics evaluated exactly, so that the results isolate the effect of sampling noise on the optimization trajectory.
quotes: After training, final test metrics are evaluated exactly.
All methods are trained for 70 optimization steps and evaluated over five independent seeds.
Thus, the reported accuracies isolate the effect of finite-shot sampling noise on the optimization trajectory, rather than confounding it with sampling noise at evaluation time.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.

assertions.value: The authors report that with exact training on setosa versus rest, Diag-QNM and DA-QNM both reach 93.33% test accuracy, compared with 91.85% for Adam.
quotes: On setosa versus rest, Diag-QNM and DA-QNM both achieve 93.33% test accuracy, compared with 91.85% for Adam.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with five seeds.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 4 gives standard errors 0.74 for Adam and 1.28 for both QNM variants; the difference is about 1.5 percentage points.

assertions.value: The authors report that with exact training on versicolor versus virginica, DA-QNM obtains the best result at 86.67%, compared with 80.56% for Adam and 83.33% for Diag-QNM.
quotes: On the harder versicolor-versus-virginica task, DA-QNM obtains the best exact-training result, reaching 86.67%, compared with 80.56% for Adam and 83.33% for Diag-QNM.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with five seeds.
assertions.reader_inference: Standard errors are 4.01 for Adam, 3.85 for Diag-QNM and 1.92 for DA-QNM, so the 6.11 point gap to Adam is about 1.5 standard errors of Adam.

assertions.value: The authors report that on setosa versus rest, Diag-QNM is the strongest method at 32 and 128 shots, reaching 52.59% and 55.56%, and suggest that a diagonal empirical geometry can provide useful stabilization when the measurement budget is limited.
quotes: On setosa versus rest, Diag-QNM is strongest at 32 and 128 shots, reaching 52.59% and 55.56%, respectively.
This suggests that a diagonal empirical geometry can provide useful stabilization when the measurement budget is limited,
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with five seeds; the explanation is the authors' suggestion.
assertions.reader_inference: All three methods are between about 44% and 56% at these budgets on a two-class task, near chance, and standard errors are 4 to 12 points; the paper does not discuss that these accuracies are close to chance.

assertions.value: The authors report that on versicolor versus virginica, Adam is the strongest method at 32 and 128 shots, reaching 45.56% and 60.00%.
quotes: On the harder versicolor-versus-virginica task, Adam remains the strongest method at 32 and 128 shots, reaching 45.56% and 60.00%, respectively.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with five seeds.
assertions.reader_inference: Adam's standard error at 128 shots is 13.33 points, larger than its lead over the other methods; at 32 shots all three are below 50%, below chance for a two-class task.

assertions.value: The authors report that with 512 shots on setosa versus rest, DA-QNM reaches 68.15%, compared with 54.81% for Adam and 60.00% for Diag-QNM, and that DA-QNM improves over Adam by 13.34 percentage points.
quotes: With 512 shots, DA-QNM reaches 68.15% on setosa versus rest, compared with 54.81% for Adam and 60.00% for Diag-QNM.
Thus, at the most informative finite-shot setting tested here, DA-QNM improves over Adam by 13.34 percentage points on setosa versus rest
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with five seeds.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 4 standard errors: 6.06 for Adam, 7.80 for Diag-QNM, 4.51 for DA-QNM. The 13.34 point gap is about two standard errors of Adam. Even the best value, 68.15%, is far below the 93.33% exact-training result on the same task.

assertions.value: The authors report that with 512 shots on versicolor versus virginica, DA-QNM reaches 63.33%, compared with 56.67% for Adam and 48.89% for Diag-QNM, and that DA-QNM improves over Adam by 6.66 percentage points.
quotes: With 512 shots, DA-QNM reaches 68.15% on setosa versus rest
On versicolor versus virginica, DA-QNM reaches 63.33%, compared with 56.67% for Adam and 48.89% for Diag-QNM.
and by 6.66 percentage points on versicolor versus virginica.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study with five seeds.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 4 standard errors: 5.09 for Adam, 10.94 for Diag-QNM, 8.39 for DA-QNM. The 6.66 point gap is smaller than the standard error of DA-QNM, so the paper's data do not resolve it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the benefit of distance-aware quantum-geometric spectral updates depends on the quality of the sampled gradient and geometry estimates, that simpler diagonal geometry or even Adam can be more robust when the shot budget is too small, and that they interpret Table 4 as finite-shot robustness evidence.
quotes: Overall, the finite-shot experiment suggests that the benefit of distance-aware quantum-geometric spectral updates depends on the quality of the sampled gradient and geometry estimates.
When the shot budget is too small, simpler diagonal geometry or even Adam can be more robust.
We therefore interpret Table 4 as finite-shot robustness evidence for the proposed optimizer,
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's interpretation of one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The text calls these results robustness evidence, while in the two-class tasks most finite-shot accuracies are between about 34% and 68%.

assertions.value: The authors state that the finite-shot results are empirical robustness evidence and not a probabilistic shot-noise guarantee, and that a full high-probability convergence analysis under shot noise is left to future work.
quotes: Finite-shot results are reported in Appendix C.5 as empirical robustness evidence, not a probabilistic shot-noise guarantee.
while leaving a full high-probability convergence analysis under shot noise to future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper itself states what its finite-shot measurement does not cover.

assertions.value: The authors state that all exact-expectation experiments use statevector simulation, that finite-shot supervised experiments use sampled observables during training, and that all optimizers are evaluated on matched task instances, matched random seeds and the same initialization whenever applicable.
quotes: All exact-expectation experiments use statevector simulation.
All optimizers are evaluated on matched task instances, matched random seeds, and the same initialization whenever applicable.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup.
assertions.reader_inference: No experiment in the paper runs on quantum hardware; the conclusion lists hardware-noisy settings as future work.

assertions.value: The authors state that future work will study scalable QFIM approximations, finite-shot theory and larger hardware-noisy settings.
quotes: Future work will study scalable QFIM approximations, finite-shot theory, and larger hardware-noisy settings.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper itself states what it leaves open.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no wall-clock time, QFIM cost or scaling with qubit count; every experiment is on a small simulated instance.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that across VQE, weighted QAOA and supervised quantum classification the strongest gains occur when spectral blocks align with circuit structure, supporting the joint use of quantum-state and circuit-structured update geometry.
quotes: Across VQE, weighted QAOA, and supervised quantum classification, the strongest gains occur when spectral blocks align with circuit structure, supporting the joint use of quantum-state and circuit-structured update geometry.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's conclusion from small simulated experiments.
assertions.reader_inference: The block-choice comparison (layer, gate, global) is reported only for QAOA in Table 2; VQE reports only the best variant and the Iris study does not vary the block choice.
